teaser: One summer, one fishing village, and a hillside that looks as if it were plugged into the mains.

lesson.text: Thirty paintings, twenty drawings and about fifty sketches. That is what André Derain reported bringing back from roughly two months in Collioure, a small port near the Spanish border, in the summer of 1905. He was 25. This hillside of olive trees is one of the thirty.

He had come because Henri Matisse, eleven years older, kept writing to him to hurry south. Derain had only recently finished his military service and was hungry to paint. The two worked side by side in a heat and a brightness that neither had known in Paris.

Derain's parents ran a dairy shop and wanted him to become an engineer. Matisse, in a proper suit, paid them a visit to argue that painting was a respectable career, and they agreed to fund their son's trip.

The southern light created a problem. It is so strong that it wipes out the soft shadows painters normally use to model form. Derain wrote that he had to learn a new idea of light: one that works by contrast between colors instead of by dark and bright. On this canvas he tries two solutions at once.

lesson.title: Two ways to put down paint
lesson.text: Compare the top of the picture with the bottom.

spots.title: Mountains in flat planes
spots.text: The sunlit slopes are smooth orange, the shaded ones a solid blue with a darker blue edge. Shadow here is not black or gray. It is simply the opposite color.

spots.title: Trees in dashes
spots.text: The olive leaves are short, separate strokes of blue, green and turquoise, laid down like a quick rain. Each stroke stays visible; none is blended into its neighbor.

spots.title: A red trunk
spots.text: The twisted trunk is painted pure vermilion red. White gaps around it are bare primed canvas, left unpainted so the colors seem lit from behind.

lesson.text: The dashes come from Vincent van Gogh and from the Neo-Impressionists, painters who built pictures out of small separate touches. The flat mountains come from Paul Gauguin, whose Tahitian canvases Derain and Matisse went to see that very summer at a collector's house nearby. Derain bolts the two together without hiding the join.
Orange against blue, red against green: Derain sets opposite colors next to each other so that each makes the other look brighter. The contrast does the work that shading used to do.

That autumn, the Collioure pictures by Matisse and Derain went on show in Paris at the Salon d'Automne, a big annual exhibition. A critic, Louis Vauxcelles, saw a traditional sculpture standing in the same room and joked that it was surrounded by “fauves,” wild beasts. The insult became the name of the movement: Fauvism.

Looking back years later, Derain described the colors of that period as charges of dynamite, meant to go off and release light. He also called Fauvism an ordeal by fire, something you pass through and come out of changed.

He did come out of it. By 1908 the dynamite was spent and Derain was painting in browns and grays. So this canvas shows a short-lived state: a young painter with new tubes of color, a new friend, and no reason yet to hold back. Wander through it and notice how fast the hand was moving.

spots.title: A green sky
spots.text: The sky is mint green with streaks of cream and pink. Since the mountains have taken the blue, the sky gets what is left.

spots.title: The peak
spots.text: The summit is split down the middle, blue on one side and orange on the other, like a folded sheet of paper catching the sun.

spots.title: Combed slope
spots.text: Long orange and yellow strokes run in parallel down the hill, following its curve. The direction of the brush tells you the shape of the land.

spots.title: A violet path
spots.text: A band of lilac dashes crosses the foreground. Violet is the opposite of the yellow-green grass, so the path seems to hum.

spots.title: The lone bush
spots.text: A low shrub in dark teal and ochre, the heaviest note in the lower half. It anchors a corner that would otherwise float away.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: Derain signed in blue at the bottom left, on a slant, in the same brisk strokes as the grass around it.

lesson.text: The painting later belonged to John Hay Whitney, an American publisher, diplomat and racehorse owner. His collection brought it to the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Go back to the number you started with. Thirty canvases in one summer means that a picture like this was probably made in a few sittings at most. The speed is not carelessness. It is the subject: a record of how intensely a place can strike you before you have had time to get used to it.

quiz.question: Where is Collioure?
options: In the south of France near Spain
quiz.explanation: It is a small port near the Spanish border where Derain joined Matisse in 1905.

quiz.question: How does Derain paint the shaded side of the mountains?
quiz.explanation: Shadow is shown by a contrasting color, blue against orange, not by darkness.

quiz.question: What are the white gaps between the strokes of the trees?
quiz.explanation: Derain left the canvas unpainted in places so the colors seem lit from behind.

quiz.question: Where does the name “Fauves” come from?
options: A critic's joke meaning wild beasts
The name of a paint brand
quiz.explanation: Louis Vauxcelles used the word at the 1905 Salon d'Automne and it stuck.

quiz.question: Which two older painters does the lesson link to the dashes and the flat planes?
quiz.explanation: The separate strokes recall Van Gogh, the flat color areas recall Gauguin.

facts.text: Derain spent about ten years in Collioure working on these paintings.
facts.explanation: He stayed roughly two months in the summer of 1905.

facts.text: Matisse helped convince Derain's parents to let him go south and paint.
facts.explanation: He visited them to argue that painting was a serious career.

facts.text: In this painting the sky is green and the tree trunk is red.
facts.explanation: Derain chose colors for contrast and intensity, not for likeness.
